translations.text: Solomon son of David became firmly established in his kingdom. The Lord his God was with him and made him greater than all the kings of the earth.
Solomon spoke to all Israel—to the commanders of thousands and hundreds, to the judges, and to all the leaders who were heads of ancestral families.
Solomon and all the people with him went to the great high place in the town of Gibeon, because the Lord’s tent of meeting, which Moses the Lord’s servant had made in the wilderness, was there.
Opposite the ark of the Lord. David had brought it up from the town of the villagers to the place David had prepared for it, for he had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem.
The bronze altar that Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, had made stood before the Lord’s tabernacle. Solomon and the whole assembly of Israel sought it out.
There Solomon went up to the bronze altar before the Lord, which was at the tent of meeting, and offered a thousand burnt offerings on it.
That night the Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream, and the Lord said to him, “Ask for something, and I will give it to you.”
Solomon said to the Lord, “You showed great kindness to my father David, and you have established me as king after him.
And now, Lord my God, let the words you spoke to David my father be fulfilled, for you have established me over this people, who are as numerous as the dust of the earth.
Now give me wisdom and knowledge so that I may lead this people in all their affairs. For who can govern this people of yours?”

The Lord said to Solomon, “Because this was in your heart, and you did not ask for possessions or honors, or for the lives of your enemies, and did not ask for many days to live, but asked for wisdom and knowledge to govern my people, over whom I have established you as king,

I am giving you wisdom and knowledge, and also what you did not ask for: wealth, possessions, and honor. None of all the kings who came before you has been like you, and none like you will arise after you.”
Solomon came to the great high place in the town of Gibeon, east of Jerusalem, from before the tent of meeting, and he reigned over all Israel.
Solomon gathered chariots and horsemen. He had fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. He stationed the chariots in the towns, and some of them were with the king in Jerusalem.
The king made silver as plentiful as stones in Jerusalem, and cedars as abundant as the sand on the seashore.
The king’s merchants bought horses for Solomon from Egypt and from the city of the Aphelites [?], purchasing them from the city of the Aphelites [?] at a price.

They brought up and bought a chariot from Egypt for six hundred pieces of silver, and a horse for one hundred and fifty. In the same way, through their agency, they exported them to all the Hittite kings and the kings of Edom.
Solomon gave orders to build a house for the name of the Lord and a royal palace for himself.
Solomon appointed seventy thousand men to carry loads, eighty thousand men to cut stone in the mountains, and thirty-six hundred supervisors over them.
Solomon sent word to Hiram king of Tyre, saying, “You showed great kindness to my father David and sent him cedars to build himself a house to live in.

Now I am building a house for the name of the Lord my God, to dedicate it to him, to offer fragrant incense before him, to keep lamps burning continually, and to offer sacrifices morning and evening, on the Sabbaths, at the new moons, and at the festivals of the Lord our God. He has decreed this for all Israel forever.
The house I am building is very great, because the Lord our God is greater than all kings.
But who has the power to build him a house? The heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain him. Who am I to build him a house, or to offer him fragrant incense?

Now send me a skilled man to work in gold, silver, bronze, iron, purple cloth, fine linen, scarlet cloth, and blue cloth, who knows how to cast molds [?], to work with the skilled craftsmen in Judah and Jerusalem whom my father David appointed.
Send me cedar, cypress, and boxwood timber from Lebanon, because I know that your servants know how to cut cedars from Lebanon. My servants will be with your servants.
Let them bring me a great deal of timber, because the house I am building is very great and magnificent.

I am bringing skilled carpenters, and I will give your servants food: twenty thousand kors of wheat, twenty thousand kors of barley, twenty thousand measures of wine, and twenty thousand measures of oil.”
Hiram king of Tyre replied in a letter that he sent to Solomon, saying, “Because the Lord loves his people, he has made you king over them.”

Hiram said, “Blessed is the Lord of lords of Israel, who created heaven and earth and gave David a wise son, knowledgeable and discerning, who conceived the plan to build a house for the Lord and a palace for his kingdom.
And now I have sent you a wise man who has understanding, Hiram.

He was the son of a widow from the tribe of Dan, and his father was a craftsman. He knows how to work in gold, silver, bronze, iron, stone, wood, purple cloth, blue cloth, fine linen, [?], and [?]; to make keys for doors; and to carry out every craft given to him by the Lord, alongside your skilled workers and the skilled workers of our lord David your father.
And now let my lord send the wheat, barley, oil, and wine that he promised to send to his servants.
We will cut cedars from Lebanon according to your wishes and your measurements, bring them to you, and put them into the Red Sea. You will take them up to Jerusalem.”
Solomon gathered all the foreign men who were in the land of Israel, following the census his father David had taken of them, and found that there were 153,600.
King Solomon assigned 70,000 of them as basket carriers, 80,000 as stonecutters in the mountains, and 3,600 as overseers to direct the people's work.
Solomon began to build the house of the Lord in Jerusalem, on the mountain of the Amorites, at the place his father David had prepared, on the threshing floor he had bought from Ornan the Jebusite.
He began construction on it in the second month of the fourth year of his reign.
These were the measurements Solomon laid out for building the house of the Lord: the house was sixty cubits long by the sacred measure, thirty cubits high, and twenty cubits wide.
He made a portico at its front. Its length across the width of the house was twenty cubits, and its height was twenty cubits. He overlaid its interior with pure gold.
He roofed the main hall with [?] wood and overlaid the ceiling of the house with fine gold. He fashioned designs of palm trees and lilies on it.
He set fine engraved ornaments in the house to beautify it and overlaid all of it with fine gold.
He overlaid the house, beginning at the front of the portico, its walls and its vestibules, with fine gold, and fashioned designs of palm trees and lilies on it.
He made the Most Holy Place. Its length across the width of the house was twenty cubits, and he overlaid it with six hundred talents of fine gold.
He also overlaid the altar with gold.
He made two cherubim of solid workmanship in the sanctuary and overlaid them with gold.
The wings of the cherubim spanned twenty cubits. One wing, five cubits long, touched the wall of the house, and the other wing, five cubits long, touched the wing of the other cherub.
One wing of the other cherub, five cubits long, touched the wall of the house, and its other wing, five cubits long, met the wing of the other cherub.
The outstretched wings of these cherubim spanned twenty cubits. They stood on their feet, with their faces turned inward.
He made a curtain of blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, worked cherubim onto it, and placed the ark behind it.
He made two pillars in front of the great house, eighteen cubits tall, and the capitals on their tops were five cubits high.
He made chains fifty cubits long and placed them on top of the pillars. He made one hundred pomegranates and fastened them to the chains.
He erected two pillars in front of the temple, one on the right and one on the left. He named the one he erected on the right Jachin, and the one on the left Boaz.
He made a bronze altar ten cubits long, ten cubits wide, and ten cubits high.
He made the cast-metal sea, ten cubits from rim to rim, square all around, and five cubits high. A cord thirty cubits long encircled it on all sides.
It stood on twelve bulls: three facing north, three facing south, three facing west, and three facing east. The Sea rested on top of them, and all their hindquarters faced inward.

Its thickness was a handbreadth, and the rim of the Sea was like the rounded rim of a cup, which was very beautiful. He made ten poles and placed five on the right and five on the left, to carry the altar of burnt offering with them.
He made ten bronze basins and placed five on the right and five on the left, for the priests to wash their hands and feet in them.
He made ten gold lampstands according to their prescribed design and placed them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left.
He also made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left. He made one hundred and twenty bowls of pure gold.
He made one large courtyard for the priests and the Levites, and overlaid the gates and bars with bronze.
He placed the Sea on the northern side, facing south.
Solomon made all these utensils in very great numbers. The weight of the bronze in these utensils that Solomon made could not be reckoned.

All the work that Solomon did in the house of the Lord was completed. Solomon brought the things his father David had dedicated—the silver, the gold, and the utensils. He gathered them, brought them in, and stored them in the treasury of the Lord.

Then Solomon gathered all the elders of Israel, the heads of the tribes, and the leaders of the ancestral families of the Israelites. They came to King Solomon in Jerusalem to bring up the ark containing the covenant of the Lord from the city of David, which is Zion.
They assembled and came to King Solomon in Jerusalem in the month of Ab, at the Festival of Shelters, in the seventh month.
All the elders of Israel came, and the priests took up the ark.
They brought up the ark of the Lord, the tent of meeting, and all the sacred utensils that were in the tent. The priests and the Levites brought them up.
King Solomon and all the people who had made themselves ready stood before the ark, sacrificing sheep and cattle too numerous to be counted or reckoned.
The priests brought the ark of the Lord and set the ark in its place in the Holy of Holies, beneath the wings of the cherubim.
The cherubim were spread out over the place of the ark, and the cherubim covered the ark and its poles from above.
Its poles were long, and their ends could be seen from beneath the ark inside the house, but they could not be seen outside. They remained there to this day.

There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed there, which he had brought down from Mount Sinai. This was the covenant that the Lord gave the Israelites when they came out of the land of Egypt.
When the priests came out of the place of service—for all the priests who were present there had entered the place of service—
the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the house of the Lord was filled with the radiance of his dwelling presence.
Then Solomon said, “Lord, you said that you would dwell in thick darkness.
I have indeed built a house for you, a place for your dwelling presence forever.”
The king turned his face and blessed all the assemblies of Israel, while all the assemblies of Israel stood.
He said, “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who spoke with his mouth to my father David and by his word confirmed what he had said:
‘Since the day I brought my people Israel out of the land of Egypt, I have not chosen for myself a city from among all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house where my name would be.
But I chose David to be king over my people Israel.’
My father David had it in his heart to build a house for the name of the Lord, the God of Israel.
The Lord said to my father David, ‘Since you had it in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well to have this in your heart.
But you will not build the house. Rather, your son, who will come from your own body, will build the house for my name.’
The Lord fulfilled the words he had spoken. I succeeded my father David and sat on the throne of Israel, just as the Lord told me, and I built a house for the name of the Lord, the God of Israel.
I prepared a place for the ark, in which is kept the covenant of the Lord that he gave to our ancestors when he brought them out of the land of Egypt.
Solomon stood before the altar of the Lord, in front of all the assemblies of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven.

Solomon had made a bronze pillar and set it up in the middle of the courtyard. It was five cubits high and two cubits wide. He had climbed up and stood on it, and he knelt on his knees while all the people of Israel watched him. He spread out his hands toward heaven in prayer, in the sight of the people of Israel.

He prayed and said, “Lord, sovereign of Israel, there is no one like you. You are the Lord who dwells in heaven above, and your wishes are carried out on the earth below. You keep your covenant and faithful love toward your servants who walk uprightly before you with all their hearts.
You kept what you promised my father David. You spoke with your mouth and fulfilled it by your will, as is evident today.

And now, Lord of lords of Israel, keep for your servant David my father what you promised him: 'You will never lack a son before me to sit on the throne of Israel, provided that your sons take care in their conduct to walk before me according to my laws, as you walked before me.'
And now, Lord, God of Israel, let the words you spoke to your servant David, my father, now be confirmed.
For in faithfulness the Lord has made his presence dwell with his people Israel on earth. Look, heaven and the highest heavens cannot contain you, much less this house that I have built.
Turn toward your servant’s prayer and his plea, Lord my God, and listen to the prayer and plea that your servant offers before you today.
Look, to be before you, knowing [?], to listen to the prayer of anyone who comes and prays before you in this house, by night and by day, this place where you said you would make your presence dwell.
Listen to the prayer of your servant and of your people Israel when they pray before you in this place. Hear from your dwelling place, from heaven; hear and forgive.
If someone wrongs his neighbor, and an oath is imposed on him to make him swear, and he comes and swears before your altar in this house,

then hear their prayer from your dwelling place, from heaven, and act. Judge your servants, condemning the guilty and bringing his conduct down on his own head, and vindicating the righteous and rewarding him according to his righteousness.
If your people Israel are defeated before their enemies because they have sinned against you, and they turn back to you, acknowledge your great name, and pray and plead before you in this house,
then hear from heaven and forgive the sins of your people Israel, and bring them back to the land you gave to them and their ancestors.

When the heavens are shut and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, and they pray before you in this place, acknowledge your great name, and turn from their sins because you afflict them,

then hear their prayer from heaven and forgive the sins of your servant and of your people Israel, teaching them your good way in which they should walk. Give rain as a blessing upon the land you gave your people as their inheritance.

When there is famine in the land, when there is pestilence, sores or suffering, flying locusts or crawling locusts, when enemies oppress them in their land and in their towns, whatever the plagues and whatever the diseases,
whatever prayer or plea anyone among all your people Israel may offer, as each endures the pain of his own heart and comes and spreads out his hands in this house,
then hear their prayers from heaven, forgive their offenses, and repay each person according to all his ways, for you know his heart. You alone know the hearts of all human beings.
Then they will fear you and walk before you in your ways all the days they live on the land you gave their ancestors.

Also concerning the foreigner who is not from your people Israel and comes from a distant country because of your name—for they will hear the fame of your great name, your mighty hand, and your uplifted arm—and they come and pray before you on that day in this house.

Hear from your dwelling place, from heaven, and do what the foreigner prays for before you, so that all the peoples of the earth may know your name and fear you as your people Israel do, and may know that your name is invoked over this house that I have built.

When your people go out to battle against their enemies by the way you send them, and pray before you toward the land you gave their ancestors, the city you chose for yourself, and the house I built for your name,
then hear their prayers and pleas from heaven and uphold their cause.

When they sin against you—for there is no human being who does not sin—and you are angry with them and hand them over to their enemies, and their captors take them captive to a land far away or nearby,
They will pray before you and turn back, and in the countries of their captors they will say, 'We have sinned, provoked anger, and done wrong.'

And they return to you with all their heart and all their soul in the cities of their captors who took them captive, and pray toward the land you gave their ancestors, the city you chose for yourself, and the house I built for your name,
then hear their prayer and their plea from your dwelling place in heaven, uphold their cause, and forgive your people who have sinned against you.
And now, my God, let your eyes be open and your ears attentive to the prayer offered in this place.
And now arise, Lord of lords, to your resting place, you and the ark of your strength. Clothe your priests with salvation, Lord of lords, and let your righteous people rejoice in your goodness.
Lord of lords, do not turn away the face of your anointed one. Remember the kindness of your servant David.
When Solomon finished praying, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offerings and sacrifices, and the glory of the Lord’s presence filled the house.
The priests could not enter the Lord’s house because the glory of the Lord’s presence had filled the house.

All the Israelites watched as the fire came down and the glory of the Lord’s presence filled the house. They fell facedown on the ground, on the pavement, and worshiped, saying to one another, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, and his kindness lasts forever.”
The king and all the people offered sacrifices to the Lord.
King Solomon offered as a sacrifice twenty-two thousand cattle and one hundred and twenty thousand sheep. So King Solomon and all the people dedicated the Lord’s house.

The priests stood at their duties, and the Levites praised the Lord with musical instruments for praise. In their praises they said, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, and his kindness lasts forever,” using David’s songs of praise. The priests praised with curved and straight horns, while all the people of Israel stood.

Solomon consecrated the middle of the courtyard in front of the Lord’s house, because he offered sacrifices and the fat of the fellowship offerings there. For the bronze altar Solomon had made was too small to hold the sacrifices, the grain offering, and the fat of the fellowship offerings.
At that time Solomon celebrated the festival for seven days, with all Israel beside him, great assemblies from Antioch to the stream of Egypt, before the Lord our God.
There were seven days for the festival and seven days for the dedication of the house; together these amounted to fourteen days.

On the day of [?] in the month of Tishri, the king sent the people away. The people blessed the king and went to their towns, rejoicing and glad at heart, giving thanks and praise for all the good things the Lord had done for David his servant, for Solomon his son, and for Israel his people.
When King Solomon finished building the Lord’s house and the king’s house, everything Solomon had intended to do in the Lord’s house and the king’s house had succeeded.
The Lord appeared to Solomon that night and said to him, “I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice.
If I choose, I will shut up the heavens so that no rain falls; if I choose, I will command the locusts to devour the land; and if I choose, I will send a plague among my people.

If my people, who are called by my name, humble themselves and pray and make their plea before me, and turn from their evil ways, then I will hear from heaven, forgive their sins, and heal their land.
Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to the prayer offered in this place.
Now I have chosen this house for myself so that my presence will be in it forever. My good deeds and my wishes will be carried out within it for all time.
As for you, if you walk before me as your father David walked, with integrity of heart and uprightness, doing everything I commanded you and keeping my commandments and my laws,
I will establish your royal throne forever, just as I swore to your father David and told him, ‘You will never lack a son before me to rule over Israel.’
But if you and your children turn away from my way and do not keep my commandments and my laws that I have set before you, and you serve the idols of the nations and worship them,
I will scatter you from the land I gave you, and this house, which I consecrated to my name, I will uproot from before me. Israel will become a proverb and a tale among all the nations.
then this house will become a ruin. Everyone who passes by it will stop, shake their head, and wave their hand, and they will say, ‘Why has the Lord done this to this great city and this house?’”

They will say, 'Because they abandoned the covenant of the Lord, the God of their ancestors, who brought them out of the land of Egypt, and went and revered the gods of the nations, served them, and bowed down to them. That is why the Lord brought these calamities upon them.'
At the end of twenty years, during which Solomon had built the Lord’s house and his royal palace,
Solomon rebuilt the towns that Hiram had given him and settled the Israelites in them.
Solomon went to Antioch, laid siege to it, and destroyed it.
He rebuilt Tadmor, which had lain ruined like a wilderness, and all the storage towns.
He rebuilt Upper Beth-horon and Lower Beth-horon.

He also built all the storage towns that belonged to Solomon, the towns for chariots, the towns for horsemen, and everything Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout the land under his rule.
As for all the people who remained of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, who were not Israelites—
their descendants who remained after them in the land, whom the Israelites had been unable to destroy, Solomon made them his slaves, laborers, and tribute-payers, as they are to this day.
But Solomon did not make any Israelites slaves in his kingdom, because they were fighting men and commanders of his chariots and horsemen.
These were the officials and overseers who served Solomon: two hundred and fifty, who directed the people doing the work.

But Solomon had brought Pharaoh’s daughter up from the city of David to the house he had built for her, because he had said, “No woman shall live with me in the house of David king of Israel, because it is holy, since the ark of the Lord entered it.”
Then Solomon offered burnt offerings and peace offerings to the Lord on the altar of the Lord that he had built in front of the portico.

He offered the required amount each day according to Moses’ command, on the Sabbaths and at the festivals three times a year: at the Festival of Unleavened Bread, the Festival of Fasting, and the Festival of Shelters.

In accordance with the ordinance of his father David, the priests were at their tasks, and the Levites at their appointed duties, praising and serving before the priests as each day required. The gatekeepers, according to their assigned duties, guarded the gates day by day, because this was what David king of Israel, who had been established as king by the Lord, had commanded.
He did not depart from anything the king had commanded him concerning the priests, the Levites, and all the service of the house.
All Solomon’s work was properly arranged, from the day the foundations of the house of the Lord were laid until the day he completed all his work.
Then Solomon went to Ezion-geber, the town opposite Eloth, on the seashore in the land of Edom.

Hiram sent his servants in ships—sailors who knew how to navigate ships at sea—with Solomon’s servants. They went to the city of Ophir, took four hundred talents of gold from there, and brought it to King Solomon.

The queen of Sheba heard of Solomon’s reputation and came to test Solomon with riddles. She came to Jerusalem with a very large retinue and camels carrying spices, a great quantity of gold, and precious stones. She came to King Solomon and told him everything that was on her mind.
King Solomon revealed everything to her, including the secrets of his heart. The king concealed nothing that he did not reveal to her.
The queen of Sheba saw Solomon’s wisdom and the house he had built,

the food at his table, the seating of his servants, the attendance of his ministers and their clothing, his cupbearers and their clothing, and the sacrifices he offered in the house of the Lord. She had no breath left to look.
She said to King Solomon, 'The report I heard in my country about your words and your wisdom was true.'
“I did not believe it until I came and saw with my own eyes. And look, you had not told me half of it! Your wisdom is greater and exceeds the report I heard.
Happy are these servants of yours who stand before you continually and hear your wisdom!

Blessed be the Lord your God, who chose you and seated you on the throne of the kingdom of Israel. Because the Lord loves Israel, he established you as king over them forever, to administer justice and righteousness.”

She gave the king one hundred and twenty talents of gold, a very great quantity of spices, and precious stones. Spices like those the queen of Sheba gave King Solomon had never been seen in the world.
The servants of Hiram and the servants of King Solomon also brought gold from Ophir and brought boxwood
for benches for the house of the Lord and for the house of King Solomon, and lyres for the singers. Nothing like them had been seen in the land of Judah.
King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she asked him for, besides what he gave her of everything she desired. Then she left and went to her own city, she and her servants.
The amount of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred and sixty-six talents of gold,
besides the taxes from the cities and the goods brought by merchants. All the kings of the Arabs and the governors of the land brought silver and gold to Solomon.
King Solomon made two hundred shields of fine gold. He overlaid each shield with six hundred darics of fine gold.
He also made three hundred shields of fine gold, using three minas of gold for the handgrip of each shield. The king placed them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
The king made a large ivory throne and overlaid it with pure gold.
The throne had six steps, and the back rim of the throne was rounded. There were armrests on either side of the seat, and two lions stood behind the armrests.
Twelve lions stood there on the six steps, on either side. Nothing like this had been made in any kingdom.
All the vessels used in King Solomon’s service were gold, and all the vessels in the king’s treasury were refined gold. Silver was considered of no value in Solomon’s days.
For King Solomon had ships that went to Tarshish with Hiram's servants. Once every three years they returned, and the ships that went to Tarshish carried silver, gold, elephants, apes, and peacocks.
King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in wealth and wisdom.
All the kings of the earth sought to see Solomon and hear the wisdom that the Lord had put in his heart.
Each of them brought him his gift: silver vessels, gold vessels, clothing, myrrh, spices, horses, and mules, in an allotted amount year after year.
Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates River to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt.
King Solomon made silver as plentiful as stones in Jerusalem, and cedars as abundant as the sand on the seashore.
They bought horses for Solomon from Egypt and from all the countries.
Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel for forty years.
Solomon rested with his ancestors, and they buried him in the city of his father David. His son Rehoboam reigned in his place.
Rehoboam went to Shechem, because all Israel had gone to Shechem to make him king.
And when Jeroboam heard
all Israel came and said to Rehoboam son of Solomon,
“Your father increased our servitude. Now lighten your father’s harsh servitude and his oppressive rule, and we will serve you.”
He said to them, “Go, and come back to me three days from now.” And the people came to him.
King Rehoboam consulted the elders who had served his father Solomon while he was alive. He said to them, 'What answer do you advise us to give this people?'

They spoke with him and said to him, “If you give these people a favorable answer, greet them with joy, and speak kindly to them, they will be good servants and workers for you all the days of your life.”
He rejected the advice of the elders who had advised him and went to consult the young men who had grown up with him and attended him.
He said to them, “What answer do you advise us to give these people who have spoken to me, saying, ‘Lighten the burden your father imposed on us, and we will serve you’?”

The young men who had grown up with him in the streets spoke to him, saying, “This is what you should say to the people who spoke to you, saying, ‘Your father made our burden heavy; you lighten our burden.’ Say this to them: ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist.’
“‘Now, my father subjected you to harsh servitude, but I will add to your burden. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with rods.’”
Jeroboam and all the people came on the third day, just as he had asked them to wait, telling them, “Come back to me on the third day.”
The king answered them harshly. King Rehoboam rejected the advice the elders had given him.

He spoke to them according to the young men’s advice, saying, “My father made your burden heavy, but I will add to your burden. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with rods.”
The people did not listen to the king, because this turn of events came from the Lord, so that the word of Ahijah the prophet from Shiloh concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat would be fulfilled.

All Israel saw that the king would not listen to them. The people answered the king, saying, “We have no share in David, nor any inheritance in the son of Jesse. Go home, everyone in Israel! Look after your own house now, David!” And Israel went home.
The Israelites living in the towns of Judah made Rehoboam king over them.
King Rehoboam sent Adoniram, who was in charge of the tax collectors, to them. But all Israel stoned him to death. King Rehoboam climbed into his chariot to flee to Jerusalem.
The Israelites have been in rebellion against the house of David to this day.

Rehoboam came to Jerusalem and assembled the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin: one hundred and eighty thousand men who drew the sword and were trained for war, to fight against Israel and restore the kingdom to Rehoboam son of Solomon.
The word of the Lord came to Shemaiah, saying to him:
“Speak to Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to the house of Benjamin, all Israel, and the rest of the people. Say to them:”
Thus says the Lord: 'Do not go up and do not fight. Return, each man to his home, for this matter has come from me.' They listened to the word of the Lord and turned back, each going to his home.
Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of the tribe of Ephraim and lived there. He went out from there and built Penuel.
Jeroboam said to himself, “The kingdom will return to the house of David.
If these people go up to offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord in Jerusalem, their hearts will turn back to their lord. They will kill me and return the kingdom to Rehoboam son of Solomon.”

The king considered the matter and made two golden calves. He said to them, “You have gone up enough! Why do you keep going up and down to Jerusalem? These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt.”
He placed one in Bethel and the other in Dan.
This became a sin, and the people went before the one calf all the way to Dan.
This matter became a sin for the whole house of Jeroboam, causing it to be uprooted and destroyed from the earth.
At that time Abijam, Jeroboam’s son, became ill.

Jeroboam said to his wife, “Please get up and disguise yourself as an ordinary woman, so that no one will know you are Jeroboam’s wife. Go to Shiloh. Ahijah the prophet is there—the one who spoke to me when I was becoming king over these people.
Go to him, and he will tell you what will happen to this boy.”
Ahijah was told by the Lord, “Jeroboam’s wife is coming to ask you for a word about her son, who is ill. Say such and such to her. When she comes in, she will be in disguise.”
When Ahijah heard the sound of her footsteps as she came through the doorway, he said to her, “Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why are you disguising yourself? I have been sent to tell you harsh things.
Go and tell Jeroboam: This is what the Lord of lords of Israel says: I raised you up from among the people and made you king over my people Israel.

I took the kingdom from the house of David and gave it to you. But you have not been like my servant David, who kept my commandments and followed my laws with all his heart, doing what was right in my sight.
You have acted more wickedly than all the kings before you. You went and made yourself idols of the nations and images, blaspheming before me, and you cast the fear of me behind your back.”

King Rehoboam son of Solomon grew strong in Jerusalem and reigned. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city the Lord had chosen from all the tribes of Israel to make his presence dwell there. His mother’s name was Naamah, from Ammon.
He did what was evil before the Lord and did not set his heart on revering the Lord and seeking him with all his heart.
These were Rehoboam’s deeds, from first to last: doing evil before the Lord, the God of Israel. There was war between Rehoboam son of Solomon and Jeroboam son of Nebat throughout his lifetime.
Rehoboam rested with his ancestors and was buried in the city of David. His son Abijah succeeded him as king.
In the eighteenth year of the reign of Jeroboam son of Nebat, Abijah became king over the tribe of Judah.
He reigned three years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Maacah, daughter of Uriel, from Ramah.

Abijah bound the fighting men—four hundred thousand young men—until they agreed to go and wage war against Jeroboam son of Nebat. Jeroboam son of Nebat gathered an army for himself and came to wage war with eight hundred thousand young men, mighty warriors.
Abijah stood on Mount Zemaraim, within the hill country of Ephraim, and said, “Listen, Jeroboam son of Nebat, and all Israel!
Surely you knew that the Lord, the God of Israel, gave David the kingship over Israel forever, to him and his sons, by a royal covenant.
But Jeroboam son of Nebat, a servant of Solomon son of David, rose up and rebelled against his master.

He gathered wicked men around him, evildoers, and grew strong against Rehoboam son of Solomon. Rehoboam was a youth, young in years, and did not know what to say. He did not comfort the people concerning the forced labor to which his father Solomon had subjected them.

And even now, what are you saying? You went and threw off the kingship of the house of David, and you went and served dead gods. I reign over one tribe, while you are many tribes, and among you are the golden calves that Jeroboam son of Nebat made for you.

You drove out the priests, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and made priests for yourselves from the people of the land. From anyone who came to present an offering, you would take a young bull and seven rams, and he would become a priest of those that are not gods.
But we have not abandoned the Lord our God. The priests who minister to the Lord are sons of Aaron, and the Levites carry out their duties.

They offered sacrifices to the Lord every morning and every evening, burned fragrant incense, and set out rows of bread on the clean tables. There were golden lampstands with their lamps, and the young lamp attendant lit them every evening. We keep the requirements of the Lord our God, but you have abandoned him. You went after dead gods, served them, and worshiped them, and abandoned the Lord,
the God of your ancestors. You too will never prosper.”
When the men of Judah raised their voices, the Lord defeated Jeroboam son of Nebat and Israel before Judah and Abijah.
The Israelites fled before the people of Judah.
Abijah inflicted a great slaughter on them, and five hundred thousand young men of Israel fell.
The Israelites were defeated at that time, and the people of Judah prevailed because they said, “Our reliance is on the Lord, the God of our ancestors.”
Abijah pursued Jeroboam and captured large towns from him: Bethel and its outlying settlements, Shelah and its outlying settlements, and Ephron and its outlying settlements.
Jeroboam’s strength diminished further during Abijah’s lifetime. The Lord struck Jeroboam, and he died.
Abijah grew strong and took fourteen wives. Twenty-six sons and sixteen daughters were born to him.
The rest of Abijah’s deeds and his ways are written in the expositions of the prophet Iddo.
Abijah rested with his ancestors, and they buried him in the City of David. His son Asa succeeded him as king. In his days the land had rest from trouble for twenty years.
Asa did what was good and right before the Lord his God.
He tore down the altars of foreign gods and the shrines, smashed the sacred pillars, and cut down the statues.
He said to Judah, “Come, let us pray before the Lord, the God of our ancestors.”
He removed the high places and idols from all the towns of Judah. His kingdom was at rest in his days, and he had no enemy among any of his neighbors.
He built fortified towns in the land of Judah, because the land was at rest. No one waged war against them during those years, because the Lord had given him rest.

He said to the people of Judah, “Come, let us build these towns and surround them with walls, towers, gates, and bars while the land is free from trouble. For we have sought the Lord our God, and he too has sought us and given us rest from all those around us. He has comforted us and rescued us.”

Asa had three hundred thousand mighty warriors from Judah who carried shields and spears, and two hundred eighty thousand from Benjamin who wore armor and drew the bow. All these were mighty warriors.
Zerah the Indian came out against them with a vast army of a million men and thirty thousand chariots. They came as far as Mareshah.
Asa went out to meet him and fought against him in the valley of Mareshah.

Asa prayed before the Lord his God and said, “You are our Lord, the helper of your people. When you deliver a vast army into the hands of a few, all the inhabitants of the world will know that we are right to trust in you. Help us, Lord our God, for in your name we have come against this great army. Lord God, do not withhold your might from us.” Then, when Asa had finished praying his prayer,
the angel of the Lord defeated the Indians before Asa and Judah, and the Indians fled.
Asa and the people with him pursued them as far as Geder. Countless Indians fell, because they were defeated before the Lord and his armies. They took and carried off a very great amount of plunder.
They devastated all the towns around Geder, because the fear of the Lord had fallen upon them. They plundered all the towns, for there was a great deal of spoil in them.
They also carried away the tents of the Arabs, captured very many sheep and camels, and brought them to Jerusalem.
A spirit from the Lord came to rest upon Azariah son of Azzur.

He went out to meet Asa and said to him, “Listen to me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin. The Lord is with you forever and ever. If you seek him, he will be found by you; but if you abandon him, he will abandon you.
For many days Israel did not serve their God faithfully, did not accept what their priests told them, and did not obey their laws. They were handed over to their enemies.
But when they were in distress, they prayed before the Lord, the God of Israel, and sought him, and he was found by them.
In those former times, when we did not fear our God, there was no peace for anyone going out or coming in, because great calamity had come upon all the inhabitants of the land.
We were scattered among every nation, among the towns and among the cities, because we had abandoned the Lord our God and were unwilling to listen to the voice of his servants the prophets.
He, in turn, repaid us for our deeds.”

When Asa heard these words of Azariah son of Azzur the prophet, he took courage and removed the idols from all the land of Judah and Benjamin and from the towns he had captured in the land of Ephraim. He renewed the altar of the Lord that stood before the railing.

He gathered all the people of Judah and the descendants of Benjamin, those from the towns he had captured in the land of Ephraim, and the foreigners living among them from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon. For many people from Israel had gathered and come to him when they saw that the Lord his God was with him.
They gathered in Jerusalem in the third month of the fifteenth year of Asa's reign.
That day they offered sacrifices to the Lord from the plunder they had brought: seven hundred cattle and six thousand sheep.
They swore oaths to pray before the Lord, the God of their ancestors, with all their heart and all their soul.
Anyone who does not pray before the LORD, the God of Israel, must die, from the least to the greatest, both men and women.
They swore an oath to the LORD with a loud voice, with curved and straight horns.

All the people of Judah rejoiced over this good news they had heard, because they had sought him with all their heart and prayed before him with all their soul. He let them find him and rescued them from all the rulers along their borders.
Asa also removed his mother Maacah from her royal position because she had held a festival for her idols. Asa cut down her idols and burned them in the Kidron Valley.
The altars were not removed from Israel. Nevertheless, Asa's heart was wholly devoted to reverence for the LORD his God throughout his life.
He brought the things his father had dedicated, and the things he himself had dedicated, into the house of the LORD: silver, gold, and utensils.
There was war in the thirty-fifth year of Asa's reign.
In the thirty-sixth year of Asa's reign, Baasha king of Israel came up against the people of Judah and fortified Ramah to prevent Asa king of Judah from going in and out.
Asa took silver and gold from the treasury of the LORD and from the royal palace and sent them to Ben-hadad king of Edom, who lived in Damascus. He said to him:

“There are sworn agreements between me and you, and between my father's house and your father's house. Look, I have sent you silver and gold. Go and break the sworn agreements you made with Baasha king of Israel, so that he will withdraw from me.”
Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent his army commanders. They came and encamped against the towns of Israel and captured Ijon, Abel Beth-maacah, and all the storehouses of the towns of Naphtali.
When Baasha heard this, he stopped building Ramah and halted all his construction work.

King Asa assembled all the people of Judah, and they took away the stones and timber of Ramah that had been prepared for Baasha's building work there. With them King Asa built Ramah of Benjamin and the town of Mizpah.

At that time Hanan the prophet came to Asa king of Judah and said to him, “Because you relied on the king of Edom and did not rely on the LORD your God, the army of Edom will therefore escape from you.

They will go and grow strong, together with the Indians and the kings who are with them. They will have very great numbers of troops, chariot teams, and horsemen. But when you seek the LORD God, he will hand them over to you.
For the eyes of the LORD look over the whole earth. Be strong, and let your hearts be wholly devoted to reverence for him. Consider all his wonders, because the LORD your God fights for you.”

Asa became angry with the seer and put him in prison, because he was speaking about things he had not seen and was unsettling the people's hearts. Because of this, Asa fled from the people at that time.
The acts of Asa, from first to last, are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
Asa was stricken in the thirty-ninth year of his reign. He became ill in his feet and collapsed inside his house.
Asa lay down with his ancestors and was buried in his tomb. He died in the forty-first year of his reign.
He was buried in David's tomb. They laid him on a bier filled with spices and made a very great fire.
His son Jehoshaphat succeeded him as king and strengthened himself against Israel.
He put mighty warriors in command in all the fortified towns of Judah and appointed governors in the land of Judah and in the land of Ephraim that his father Asa had captured.
The LORD was with Jehoshaphat because he followed the earlier ways of his ancestor David and did not pray to idols.
For he prayed to the LORD, the God of his father, followed his commandments, and kept his laws. He did not act as Israel did.
The Lord established the kingdom in his hands, and all the people of Judah gave gifts to Jehoshaphat. He had very great wealth and honor.
His heart grew strong in the ways of the Lord, and he also removed the altars and high places that were within the territory of Judah.
In the third year of his reign, he sent for his officials and military commanders—Obadiah, Zechariah, Mattanel, and Malchiah—to teach in the towns of Judah.
With them were the Levites Shemaiah, Mattaniah, Zechariah, Asahel, Nattura, Jonathan, Adonijah, and Tobiah. All these were Levites, and with them were the priests Elishama and Jehoram.
They taught throughout the land of Judah, and they had with them the book of the law of the Lord. They traveled around all the towns of Judah and taught the people.
The fear of the Lord came upon all the kingdoms of the lands surrounding Judah, and they did not fight against Jehoshaphat.

From the Philistine cities they brought Jehoshaphat silver, gifts, and a poll tax. The Arabs also brought flocks: seven thousand seven hundred rams and seven thousand seven hundred male goats in a single year.
Jehoshaphat continued to grow wealthier until he became very rich. He built fortresses and storage towns in Judah.
He had extensive enterprises in the land of Judah, and warriors, mighty fighting men, in Jerusalem.
This was their number according to their ancestral houses in Judah, with their commanders of thousands: Gaddino, the mighty warrior, had three hundred thousand mighty fighting men serving under him.
Johanan, the commander, had two hundred eighty thousand mighty fighting men serving under him.
After him was Shimei son of Zerah, who pleased the Lord. With him were two hundred thousand valiant fighting men.
From Benjamin there were mighty fighting men under a man named Eliada. Two hundred thousand men who shot with bows and carried shields served under him.
Jehozabar, the mighty warrior, had one hundred eighty thousand fighting men serving under him.
All these served King Jehoshaphat, apart from those whom the king put in charge of the fortified towns throughout the land of Judah.
Jehoshaphat had very great wealth and honor, and he formed close ties with Ahab.
After two years he went down to Ahab in Samaria. Ahab slaughtered a very large number of sheep and cattle for him and for the troops with him, and urged him to go up to Ramoth-gilead.

Ahab king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, “Will you go up with me to Ramoth-gilead?” He answered him, “I will go up. I am like you, my people are like your people, and my horses are like your horses. I will go with you into battle.”
Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, “Please inquire today for the word of the Lord.”

The king of Israel gathered the prophets, about four hundred men, and said to them, “Shall we go to battle at Ramoth-gilead or not?” They said to him, “Go up, and the Lord will deliver your enemies into your hands.”
King Jehoshaphat said, “Is there a true prophet of the Lord here whom we can consult?”

The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “There is still one man through whom we can inquire for the word of the Lord, but I hate him, because he does not prophesy anything good about me, only evil. His name is Micaiah son of Imlah.” Jehoshaphat said, “The king should not say that.”
The king of Israel called for an official and said to him, “Hurry! Bring Micaiah son of Imlah.”

The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were sitting, each on his throne, wearing embroidered robes. They were seated at the gate of Samaria, and all the false prophets were prophesying before them.
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made himself iron horns and said to him, “This is what the Lord says: With these you will gore the Edomites until you finish them off and destroy them.”
All the prophets were prophesying in the same way, saying, “Go up to Ramoth-gilead and conquer it! The Lord will deliver your enemies into your hands, O king.”

The messenger who went to summon Micaiah spoke with him and said, “Look, the words of the false prophets agree in speaking good things before the king. Let your words be favorable like those of one of them, and prophesy good things yourself.”
Micaiah said, “As the Lord God lives, I will speak only what my God puts into my heart.”
He went to the king, and the king said to him, “Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead or not?” He said to him, “Go up and conquer it, and they will be handed over to you.”
The king said to him, “How many times must I put you under oath to tell me nothing but the truth in the name of the Lord?”
He said, “I saw all Israel scattered among the mountains, like sheep without a shepherd. And the Lord said, ‘These people have no king. Let each man return home in peace.’”
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Did I not tell you that this man prophesies nothing good about me, but only evil?”
Micaiah said, “Therefore, hear the word of the Lord: I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, with all the armies of heaven standing at his right and at his left.
The Lord said, ‘Who will entice Ahab king of Israel to go up and be killed at Ramoth-gilead?’ One said, ‘I will entice him,’ and another said, ‘I will entice him.’
Then a spirit came forward, stood before the Lord, and said, ‘I will entice him.’ The Lord said to him, ‘How?’
He said, ‘I will go out and become a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.’ The Lord said to him, ‘You will entice him, and you will succeed. Go out and do as you have said.’
Now, look: the Lord has put a lying spirit in the mouths of all these prophets of yours, and the Lord has decreed disaster against you.”
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah came forward, struck Micaiah on the cheek, and said to him, “Since when has the Spirit of the Lord passed from me to speak with you?”
Micaiah said, “You will see on that day when you go into an inner room to hide.”
The king of Israel said, “Take Micaiah away and confine him in the house of Amon, the governor of the city, and in the house of Joash, the king’s son.
Say, ‘This is what the king says: Put this man in prison, and give him only enough bread and water to keep him alive until I return in peace.’”
Micaiah said, “If you do return and come back in peace, the Lord has not spoken with me.” And he said, “Listen, all you peoples!”
Jehoshaphat king of Judah and Ahab king of Israel went up to Ramoth-gilead.

The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “I will arm myself and come and take my place in the battle line, but you put on your armor.” So the king of Israel armed himself and went in and took his place in the battle line.
The king of the Edomites commanded his thirty-two chariot commanders, saying to them, “Do not fight anyone, small or great, but only the king of Israel.”
When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they said, “This is the king of Israel,” and came against him to fight him. Jehoshaphat cried out, and the Lord helped him and drew them away from him.
When the chariot commanders saw that Jehoshaphat was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him.

A man shot his bow in his direction without knowing whom he was aiming at, and struck the king of Israel at a joint in his armor. The king said to his chariot driver, “Turn around and take me out of the camp, because I have been mortally wounded.”
The battle [?] grew fierce that day, and the king of Israel remained seated in his chariot, fighting the Edomites until evening. He died at sunset.
Toward evening, Jehoshaphat returned safely to his home in Jerusalem.
The son of Hanan the seer went out to meet him and said to King Jehoshaphat, “You went to help the wicked and loved those who hate the Lord. Because of this, the Lord is angry with you.
But I am confident that good words have been heard from you, because you have not shed innocent blood in the land, and you have set your heart on praying sincerely before the Lord.”

Jehoshaphat lived in Jerusalem. He went out again, traveling from the city of Beersheba as far as the hill country of Ephraim, and brought the people back to reverence for the Lord, the God of their ancestors.
He appointed judges in the land, in all the fortified towns of Judah and in the strong towns.
He said to the judges, “Consider what you are doing, because you are judging not for human beings but for the Lord our God. Be strong and judge truthfully, and may the Lord be with you forever.”
Be careful and act accordingly, because there is no injustice, partiality, or acceptance of bribes with the Lord our God.
In Jerusalem also, Jehoshaphat appointed some of the Levites, priests, and heads of the ancestral families of the Israelites to administer the Lord’s justice. Then he returned to Jerusalem.
He instructed them, saying, “This is how you must act: in the fear of the Lord, faithfully and wholeheartedly.

“In every case that comes to you from your fellow Israelites who live in your towns, whether concerning bloodshed or concerning a law, a commandment, or a judgment, warn them not to incur guilt before the Lord, lest he become angry with them and their fellow Israelites. Do this, and you will not incur guilt.

“Look, I have appointed priests over you to render true and faithful judgments according to the Lord’s command.” Zechariah son of Shemaiah made all the king’s commands known to everyone of the house of Judah. He also made them known to the scribes and Levites, and repeated everything before them, saying to them, “Be strong and act, and may the Lord be your help forever.”
After these things, the Moabites and Ammonites came, along with men skilled in warfare, to wage war against Jehoshaphat.
People came and told Jehoshaphat, “A great army is coming against you from beyond the Red Sea. They are now camped at Jericho, that is, En Gedi.”
Jehoshaphat was afraid and lifted his face to pray before the Lord. He proclaimed a fast for everyone of the house of Judah and told them, “Be strong, and come, let us appeal to the Lord our God.”
Everyone of the house of Judah gathered and came, even from distant towns, to appeal to the Lord.
Jehoshaphat stood among the people of Judah in the Lord’s house in Jerusalem, in front of the new gate.
He prayed, saying, “Lord, God of our ancestors, you are God in heaven, and you rule over all the kingdoms of the world. Power and might are yours, and I stand before you in prayer.
“You are our God. You destroyed the inhabitants of this land before your people Israel and gave it forever to the descendants of Abraham, your friend.
“They settled in it and built a sanctuary in it for your name, saying,

“‘Now that the sanctuary is among us, no disaster will come upon us—neither sword, nor judgment, nor plague, nor famine. We will come and stand before this house and before you, because your name has been invoked over this house. We will pray before you in this house, and you will hear the sound of our prayer and save us.’

“And now, here are the Ammonites, Mount Gebal, and Moab, whom you did not allow Israel to engage with, because you brought them out of the land of Egypt and freed them from enslavement to the Egyptians.
“Look, they are repaying us with harm and coming to drive us out of the inheritance you gave us.

“Lord our God, reveal yourself and judge them, because we have no strength to stand against them. Bring the sword of your judgment upon them. We do not know what to do, but our eyes are lifted toward you.”
Everyone of the house of Judah stood before the Lord, along with their little children, wives, sons, and daughters.

The spirit of courage from the Lord rested upon Hazael son of Zechariah, son of Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, son of Mattaniah, a Levite from the descendants of Asaph, while he was standing before the people of Israel.

He said, “Listen, all Judah, inhabitants of Jerusalem, and King Jehoshaphat. This is what the Lord your God says: Do not be afraid or terrified of this great army, because the battle is not yours; the battle belongs to the Lord.
“Hurry and go down against them. They are coming up the ascent at dawn, and you will find them at the cliff of the valley, before the wilderness.

“They are coming up to fight with you. At that time, stand and see the deliverance the Lord will bring about for you, people of the house of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem. Do not be afraid or terrified. Tomorrow go out to meet them, and Adonai, the Lord of lords, will be your help.”
Jehoshaphat fell face down on the ground and worshiped. Everyone of the house of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem also fell down and worshiped before the Lord.
The Levites from the descendants of Kohath and the descendants of Korah stood up to praise the Lord, the God of Israel, with a loud voice.

They rose early in the morning and went out to the wilderness of Tekoa. As they went out, Jehoshaphat stood and said, “Listen to me, people of the house of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem. Trust in the Lord your God, and you will be made secure. Trust in his prophets, and you will be saved.”

He stood among the people and said, “Come, let us give thanks to the Lord and praise the splendor of his holiness, as he goes out before our armies and wages war for us against our enemies.” They said, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, and his kindness lasts forever.” The hills began to sing praise, and the mountains began to rejoice.
Judah came to the mountain of the lookouts in the wilderness. They looked, and there were all their bodies, dead and lying on the ground. Not one of them had escaped.

Jehoshaphat and the people of Israel came to take their plunder. Among them they found a very great amount of plunder, possessions, herds of horses, and desirable objects. They took whatever they wanted. After three days they had taken the plunder, for it was very abundant.
On the fourth day they gathered in the Valley of Blessing, because there they blessed the Lord their God. That is why that place has been called Blessing to this day.
All the people of Judah returned to Jerusalem, with Jehoshaphat at their head. They came to Jerusalem with great joy, because the Lord had made them rejoice over their enemies.
They came to Jerusalem with songs of praise, harps, and curved and straight horns, and they came to the house of the Lord.
Fear of the Lord fell on all the cities and their kingdoms when they heard that the Lord was fighting against Israel's enemies.
Jehoshaphat's kingdom was at rest from [?], and God gave him rest from all his neighbors.
Jehoshaphat became king over Judah. He was thirty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for twenty-five years. His mother's name was Arubah, the daughter of Shilhi.
He followed all the ways of his father Asa and did not turn away from them, doing what was right before the Lord.
However, he did not remove the high places, which remained until then, and the people did not set their hearts on the God of their ancestors.
The rest of Jehoshaphat’s deeds, from first to last, are written in the accounts of Jehu son of Hanani, which are recorded in the book of the kings of Israel.
After these things, Jehoshaphat king of Judah allied himself with Ahaziah king of Israel, that wicked man who did more evil than all the kings of Israel.
He allied himself with him to build ships to sail to Tarshish, and he built ships in the city of Ezion-geber.

Eliezer son of Dodo, in the city of Mareshah, prophesied against Jehoshaphat and said to him, "Because of your partnership with Ahaziah, the Lord has ruined all your work." The ships were wrecked, and he could not go to Tarshish.
Jehoshaphat rested with his ancestors and was buried beside his ancestors in the City of David. His son Jehoram succeeded him as king.
He had brothers, sons of Jehoshaphat, whose names were Azariah, Nahuel, Zechariah, Azariah, Malchiel, and Shephatiah. All these were sons of Jehoshaphat king of Judah.
Their father gave them many gifts of silver and gold, many other gifts, and fortified cities in Judah. But the kingdom was given to Jehoram because he was his oldest son.
Jehoram took over his father's kingdom and established his power. He killed all his brothers in battle and also killed some of the elders of Israel.
He was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eight years.
He followed the ways of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, because Ahab's sister was his wife. He did what was evil before the Lord.
But the Lord was unwilling to destroy the house of David because of the oath he had sworn to David, to give him and his sons a shining lamp forever.
In his days the Edomites rebelled against Judah's rule and appointed a king over themselves.
Jehoram crossed over with his commanders and all his chariots. When he rose during the night, they ravaged the Edomites, and the commanders of the chariots came to him.

The Edomites rebelled against Judah's rule and have remained independent to this day. At that time the Edomites living in Libnah also rebelled against his rule, because he had abandoned the Lord, the God of his ancestors.
He also made high places in the hill country of Judah, gave wine to Jerusalem’s Nazirites to drink, and scattered the people of Judah.

Some words from Elijah the prophet were brought to him, saying, "This is what the Lord, the God of your ancestor David, says: Because you have not followed the ways of your father Jehoshaphat or the ways of Asa king of Judah,

but have followed the ways of the kings of Israel and led Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray into the prostitution of the house of Ahab, and have also killed your brothers, your father's sons, who were better than you,
the Lord is about to strike you, your people, your children, your wives, and all your possessions with a great blow.
You yourself will die of a severe illness and perish in great torment, until your intestines come out because of your illness. For many years you will waste away in torment."
The Lord will stir up against Joram the spirit of the Philistines and of the Arabs who live among the Indians.

They will march against Judah and devastate it. They will carry away everything found in the king’s palace, including his sons and his wives. No male child will be left to him except Ahaziah, his youngest son.
After all these things, a disease will afflict his bowels. He will die from a severe illness, and there will be no cure for him.

After many days, when the prophet’s word was fulfilled at the end of two years, his bowels came out because of his illness, and he died from a terrible disease. The people did not honor him as they had honored his ancestors.

He was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eight years. He died without anyone regretting his loss, and he was buried in the city of his ancestor David, but not in the royal tombs.

The inhabitants of Jerusalem made his son Ahaziah king after him, because the army had killed all his older sons when the Arabs came and devastated the camps. So Ahaziah son of Jehoram, king of Judah, became king.
Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for one year. His mother’s name was Athaliah, daughter of Omri.
He followed the ways of the house of Ahab, because he was Ahab’s nephew, and he too sinned greatly.
He did evil before the Lord, like the house of Ahab, because after his father died they became his advisers, to his destruction.
He followed their advice and went with Joram son of Ahab, king of Israel, to fight against Hazael king of Edom at Ramoth-gilead. The Edomites wounded Joram.

He returned to Jezreel to recover from the wound they had inflicted on him at Ramoth while he was fighting Hazael king of Edom. Ahaziah went down to see Joram son of Ahab in Jezreel because he was ill.
Ahaziah’s downfall through his coming to Joram was from the Lord. When he arrived, he went out with Joram to meet Jehu son of Nimshi, whom the Lord had anointed to destroy the house of Ahab.
Then, while Jehu was carrying out judgment against the house of Ahab, he found the officials of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah’s brothers who were attending Ahaziah, and he killed them.

He searched for Ahaziah and captured him while he was hiding in Samaria. He had him brought to him, killed him, and buried him, because he said, “He is a descendant of Jehoshaphat, who prayed to the Lord with all his heart.” There was no one left in the house of Ahaziah with the strength to uphold the kingdom.
When Athaliah, Ahaziah’s mother, saw that her son was dead, she rose up and destroyed all the royal sons of the house of Judah.

But Jehosheba, the king’s daughter, took Joash son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the royal sons who were being killed. She hid him and his nurse in her bedroom. Jehosheba, daughter of King Joram and wife of Jehoiada the priest, hid him from Athaliah because she was Ahaziah’s sister, and they did not kill him.
He remained hidden with her in the house of the Lord for six years, while Athaliah ruled over the land.

In the seventh year, Jehoiada took courage and brought together the commanders of hundreds: Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of Jehohanan, Azariah son of Obed, Shemaiah son of Iddo, and Elishaphat son of Zichri. All these entered into an oath
to travel throughout Judah. He gathered the Levites from all the towns of Judah and the heads of the ancestral families of Israel, and they came to Jerusalem.
All the people swore an oath before the king in the house of the Lord. He said to them, “Here is the king’s son. He will rule over you, just as the Lord said concerning his servant David.
This is what you must do: half of you—the priests, Levites, and gatekeepers coming on duty on the Sabbath—
and a third at the king’s palace, and a third at the Butchers’ Gate. All the people are to keep watch in the courtyard of the house of the Lord.
No one is to enter the house of the Lord except the priests and Levites. They may enter because they are holy. All the people are to keep watch over the house of the Lord.
The Levites are to bring the king out, surrounding him, each man with his weapons in his hand. Anyone who enters the inner house must die. Stay with the king when he comes in and when he goes out.”

The Levites and all the people of Judah did as Jehoiada the priest had commanded them. Each man took his companions, those who were on guard duty when the Sabbath began together with those who were on guard duty when the Sabbath ended, because Jehoiada the priest had released them from their guard duties.
Jehoiada the priest gave the commanders of hundreds the spears, bucklers, and shields of King David that were in the house of the Lord.
All the people took their positions, each beside the left side of the house, and by the altar and the house, and they surrounded the king.
They brought out the king’s son and put the crown and [?] on his head, and established him as king. Jehoiada and his sons anointed him and said, “Long live the king!”
Athaliah heard the sound of the people rejoicing and praising the king, and she came to the king at the house of the Lord.

She looked, and there was the king standing by the pillar, as was customary for kings. Curved and straight horns were sounding before the king, and all the people were rejoicing, sounding horns, and singing songs of praise. Athaliah tore her clothes and said, “Treason! Treason!”

Jehoiada the priest commanded the commanders of hundreds who were in charge of the army, saying to them, “Take her outside the ranks, and whoever follows her is to be killed with the sword.” For the priest had said, “She must not die in the house of the Lord.”
They made room for her, and she went along the road to the horses’ entrance and died there.
Jehoiada swore an oath between himself, all the people, and the king, that they would be the Lord’s people.
All the people of Israel entered the temple of Baal and demolished it. They thoroughly smashed its altars, crushed its images, and killed the priest of Baal before the altar.

Jehoiada appointed officials in the house of the Lord, together with the priests and Levites whom David had assigned to keep watch over the house of the Lord, to offer burnt offerings as written in the law of Moses, with joy and songs of praise, under David’s direction.
The gatekeepers were to stand at the gates of the house of the Lord, so that no unclean people would enter there.
They took the commanders of hundreds, the leaders of the people, and all the people of the land, and came through the upper gate of the king’s palace. They seated the king on the royal throne.
All the people of the land rejoiced and sounded horns in praise, and they killed Athaliah with the sword.
Joash was seven years old when he became king, and he reigned for forty years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zibiah, from the city of Beersheba.
Joash did what was right before the Lord throughout the lifetime of Jehoiada the priest.
Jehoiada took two wives for him, and he fathered sons and daughters.
After these things, he privately agreed with Joash to restore the house of the Lord and repair everything in it that needed attention.

Jehoiada gathered the priests and Levites and said to them, “Go out to the towns of Judah and collect silver and gold from all the towns of Israel, and repair the house of your God year after year. You must hurry to complete the work.”

The king summoned Jehoiada the elder and said to him, “Why do you not require the Levites to go and bring from Judah and Jerusalem the offerings of Moses, the Lord’s servant? Gather Israel to the tent of meeting.”
Athaliah had been teaching the children wickedness and had broken into the house of the Lord. She had even turned all the holy people who were in the house of the Lord into idol worshipers.
The king gave the command, and they made a chest and placed it outside the gate of the house of the Lord.
They proclaimed in Judah and Jerusalem that people should bring to the Lord the contribution that Moses, the Lord’s servant, had commanded in the wilderness.
All the leaders and all the people rejoiced and brought their contributions. They made a chest and set it in place, and they put their contributions into it until it was full.
When they saw that there was a large amount of silver in the chest, the king’s secretary and the chief steward of the high priest came in, counted the silver, and tied it into bags.

They gave it to those doing the work on the house of the Lord. They hired stonecutters and carpenters to repair the house of the Lord, as well as workers in iron and bronze to repair the house of the Lord.
Jehoiada grew old and lived a full life, and he died at the age of one hundred and thirty.
They buried him in the City of David, in the tomb of the kings, and said, “This is how someone who has done good in Israel and made great efforts for the house of the Lord should be repaid.”
After Jehoiada died, the leaders of Judah came and bowed down to the king, because he listened to them.
They abandoned the house of the Lord, the God of their ancestors, and went and worshiped images and idols. Wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem because they had committed this sin.
He sent messages to them through prophets to turn them back from their ways, but they did not listen. He warned them, but they did not accept it.

The Spirit of the Lord clothed Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest. He went up and stood above the people and said to them, “This is what the Lord says: Why have you transgressed the Lord’s commandments? You will not prosper. Because you have abandoned my way, I too am abandoning you.”
They rebelled against him and stoned him at the king’s command in the courtyard of the LORD’s house.

King Joash did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada the priest, their father, had shown him, but killed his sons after him. As his sons were being killed, they said, “May the LORD see and demand an accounting.”
At the end of the year, the army of Edom advanced against him and came against Judah and Jerusalem. They destroyed all the leaders of the people and sent all their captives to the king in Damascus.

Although the men who came with the army of Edom were few, the Lord delivered a very large army into their hands because they had abandoned the Lord, the God of their ancestors. The judges rejected what Joash had done.

When they departed from him, having left him seriously ill, his servants plotted against him because of the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest. They killed him on his bed, and he died. They buried him in the city of David his ancestor, but they did not bury him in the burial place of the kings.
These are the names of the men who plotted against him: Zabur son of Shimeath the Ammonite woman, and Jehozabar son of Natrath the Moabite woman.
His sons, the many men who plotted against him, and the rest of the sins he committed in the LORD’s house are recorded in the commentaries on the Book of Kings. His son Amaziah became king after him.
Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother’s name was Jehoaddan, from Jerusalem.
He did what was right before the LORD, but not with an undivided heart.
When his hold on the kingdom became strong, he killed the servants who had killed his father the king.

But he did not kill the murderers’ children, because it is written in the book of the law of Moses, as the LORD commanded: “Fathers must not be put to death because of their children, and children must not be put to death because of their fathers. Each person must die for his own sins.”

Amaziah gathered the people of Judah and organized them by their ancestral families under commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds, throughout Judah and Benjamin. He counted those twenty years old and upward and found three hundred thousand young men fit to go to war, who wielded swords and carried shields.
He also hired one hundred thousand mighty warriors from Israel for one hundred talents of silver.
A prophet of the LORD came to him and said to the king, “Do not let the army of Israel go with you, because the LORD is not with Israel or with any of the people of Ephraim.
For if you go into battle to wage a great war, the LORD will cast you down before your enemies, because you have not praised the LORD, who is the helper and the one who raises people up.”

Amaziah said to the prophet of the LORD, “What folly have I committed in giving these hundred talents to the men of Israel?” The prophet of God said to him, “The Lord your God can give you much more than this, many times what you gave.”

Amaziah dismissed the men who had come to him from Ephraim to go back to their own place. His anger burned fiercely against the people of Israel, and he sent them back to their own place in his furious anger.
Amaziah took courage, led his people, and went to the Valley of Salt. He killed and destroyed ten thousand of the inhabitants of Mount Gebal.
The people of Judah captured ten thousand alive and brought them to the top of the rock. They all came bound in chains.

The sons of the warriors whom Amaziah had captured when he went to battle were given authority by him over the towns of Judah, among the Samaritans, and over the towns of the nations. They slaughtered three thousand from those towns and took a great deal of plunder.
After Amaziah returned from attacking the Edomites, they brought him the gods of the inhabitants of Mount Gebal. He set them up before him, bowed down before them, and offered them fragrant incense.
The LORD became angry with Amaziah and sent a prophet to him, who said, “Why have you prayed before the gods of the nations, who could not rescue their worshipers from your hands?”

While the prophet was speaking with him, he said to him, “The worship of wooden objects has been granted to the king.” The prophet withdrew from him and said to him, “Woe to you! The LORD has devised a disastrous plan against you to destroy you, and you have not listened to my voice.”
King Amaziah of Judah took counsel and sent word to Joash son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, “Come, let us face one another.”

Jehoash king of Israel sent word to Amaziah king of Judah, saying, “The thornbush in Lebanon sent word to the cedar in Lebanon, saying, ‘Give your daughter to my son as his wife.’ But a wild animal in Lebanon passed by and trampled the thornbush.

You have indeed devastated the Edomites, and because of this your heart has grown proud. Enjoy your honor and stay at home. Why are you eager for disaster, so that you fall, and the people of Judah with you?”
But Amaziah would not listen.
Joash king of Israel went up, and they went up and faced one another at Beth-shemesh, a town within the territory of Judah.

Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah at the town of Beth-shemesh and brought him to Jerusalem. He broke down four hundred cubits of Jerusalem's wall, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate.
